This study investigates levels of cuproptosis markers in Wilson disease (WD) and their role in the occurrence and development of WD. We retrospectively collected clinical data from 76 patients with Leipzig score ≥ 4 hospitalized in the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui University of Chinese Medicine from January 2023 to September 2023. The participants were given copper chelators (sodium dimercaptosulphonate (20 mg·kg −1 ), 4 courses of treatment, 32 days). The levels of clinical indicators (ALT, AST, ALP, HA, LN, PIIINP, CIV, liver stiffness measurement, United Wilson disease rating scale), oxidative stress indexes (SOD, MDA, GSH), cuproptosis markers (FDX1, DLAT, LIAS, ACO-2, SDHB, PLOD1, DPYD) of the participants were measured before and after treatment. Compared with the control group, FDX1, DLAT, DPYD, and POLD1 in WD were significantly up-regulated before treatment (6464.34 ± 2980.66 vs 4125.43 ± 2230.13 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 1364.36 ± 376.81 vs 884.22 ± 175.42 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 279.74 ± 123.63 vs 155.68 ± 67.32 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 3536.11 ± 1404.83 vs 1487.76 ± 658.26 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001), while SDHB was significantly down-regulated (2458.75 ± 1103.75 vs 5338.22 ± 921.54 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .05). SOD was significantly down-regulated before treatment (13.20 ± 2.06 vs 13.27 ± 1.79 U ⋅ mgprot −1 , P < .05), while MDA and GSH were significantly up-regulated (10.53 ± 4.76 vs 4.92 ± 1.81 nmol ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 49.28 ± 25.55 vs 24.70 ± 12.01 µol ⋅ L −1 , P < .001). POLD1 were down-regulated (3536.11 ± 1404.83 vs 1487.76 ± 658.26 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001), and SDHB was up-regulated after treatment (2458.75 ± 1103.75 vs2709.61 ± 906.95 pg ⋅ mL −1 , P < .05), while SOD, MDA and GSH were significantly down-regulated (13.20 ± 2.06 vs 12.48 ± 1.52 U ⋅ mgprot −1 , P < .05, 10.53 ± 4.76 vs 7.65 ± 3.65 nmol ⋅ mL −1 , P < .001, 49.28 ± 25.55 vs 34.09 ± 15.02 µmol ⋅ L −1 , P < .001). The expression levels of cuproptosis markers and oxidative stress indexes are abnormal in WD patients. Introduction Hepatolenticular degeneration, also known as the Wilson disease (WD), is induced by ATP7B gene mutation, which causes partial or complete loss of function of the copper-transporting P-type ATPase. As a result, excess Cu 2+ cannot be transported out of the cell, resulting in excessive Cu 2+ deposition in the liver, brain, kidney, cornea, and other tissues, thus causing diseases. WD causes brain degeneration and is mainly characterized by liver cirrhosis and basal ganglia damage. The clinical manifestations of WD mainly include progressively worsening extrapyramidal symptoms, psychiatric symptoms, cirrhosis of the liver, renal impairment, and corneal pigment rings. [ 1 ] Copper is one of the essential trace elements in the human body. Free Cu 2+ is a cofactor or key component of more than 30 enzymes and copper-containing proteins in the body, which plays an important role in many physiological processes, such as mitochondria metabolism and the maintenance of oxidation-reduction homeostasis. [ 2 ] Studies have demonstrated that Cu 2+ destabilizes the accumulation of lipoacylated proteins and iron-sulfur cluster protein by directly binding to lipoacylated parts in the tricarboxylic acid cycle, leading to protein toxicity stress, thus inducing apoptosis-independent cell death. Furthermore, excessive Cu 2+ can lead to abnormal cell function and promote the generation of reactive oxygen species, inducing Haber - Weiss reaction and subsequent Fenton reaction, leading to copper-related cuproptosis and iron-related ferroptosis. [ 3 , 4 ] Tsvetkov et al explored liver pathology in Atp7b-homozygous (Atp7b−/−), Atp7b heterozygous (Atp7b−/+), and wild-type mice and found that copper overload results in the same cellular effects as cuproptosis, characterized by accumulation of lipoacylated proteins and iron-sulfur cluster protein instability. [ 5 ] Xu et al suggested that the absence of iron-sulfur proteins and lipoacylated proteins induces mitochondria damage, further inducing cell death. [ 6 ] However, the role of Cu 2+ carriers in cell death in WD disease progression and diagnosis is unknown. This study aimed to investigate the expression levels of cuproptosis markers in WD and explore their roles in the occurrence and development of WD. Therefore, this study may provide references for clinical diagnosis and treatment of WD.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the expression characteristics of cuproptosis markers, oxidative stress indexes, copper metabolism, and hepatic fibrosis in Wilson disease patients, concluding that conventional chelation therapy significantly improves these abnormal markers and may reverse hepatic fibrosis progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Conventional chelation therapy using sodium dimercaptosulphonate (DMPS)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Sodium dimercaptosulphonate (DMPS) at 20 mg 7kg 7−1 was administered intravenously once daily for 6 days per course, dissolved in 5% glucose or 0.9% sodium chloride solution, with calcium gluconate (20 mL) given intravenously once daily for 2 days during intervals. This regimen consisted of four 8-day courses of treatment, totaling 32 days; no dose-response comparisons were reported.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An iron-sulfur protein and a subunit of succinate dehydrogenase, involved in the respiratory chain and tricarboxylic acid cycle, crucial for energy metabolism. Its loss is induced by copper, playing a role in cuproptosis and mediates the oxidation of succinic acid.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Wilson disease (WD) before and after chelation therapy.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Down-regulation before treatment indicates disorder of iron-sulfur proteins, affecting succinic acid metabolism and mitochondrial energy. Up-regulation after treatment suggests restoration of mitochondrial metabolic pathway to normal, alleviating disorders related to Wilson disease and improving iron-sulfur cluster protein stability.
